payload.markdown: I can use the Strategy pattern to compose my way out of trouble. Strategy is used to move a set of algorithms into a separate type. By moving cost calculations, I can simplify the Lesson type. You can see this in Figure 8-4.

payload.markdown: The Lesson class requires a CostStrategy object, which it stores as a property. The Lesson::cost() method simply invokes CostStrategy::cost(). Equally, Lesson::chargeType() invokes CostStrategy::chargeType(). This explicit invocation of another object’s method in order to fulfill a request is known as delegation. In my example, the CostStrategy object is the delegate of Lesson. The Lesson class washes its hands of responsibility for cost calculations and passes on the task to a CostStrategy implementation. payload.markdown: As you can see, one effect of this structure is that I have focused the responsibilities of my classes. CostStrategy objects are responsible solely for calculating cost, and Lesson objects manage lesson data. So, composition can make your code more flexible because objects can be combined to handle tasks dynamically in many more ways than you can anticipate in an inheritance hierarchy alone. There can be a penalty with regard to readability, though. Because composition tends to result in more types, with relationships that aren’t fixed with the same predictability as they are in inheritance relationships, it can be slightly harder to digest the relationships in a system.

items: Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Composition: Building classes from other objects instead of inheriting from them.
Inheritance: Deriving a class from a base class to reuse and specialise its behaviour.
Strategy Pattern: Swapping an algorithm behind a common interface at runtime.
foreach: The default loop for walking arrays and Traversable objects.
Constructor Property Promotion: Declaring constructor parameters as properties in a single step (PHP 8).
Data Mapper: A layer that moves objects to and from storage without the object knowing SQL.

8370.code:
<?php

{

   Here is the CostStrategy class, together with its implementing children:

// listing 08.09
abstract class CostStrategy
{
    abstract public function cost(Lesson $lesson): int;
    abstract public function chargeType(): string;
}

// listing 08.10
class TimedCostStrategy extends CostStrategy
{
    public function cost(Lesson $lesson): int
    {
        return ($lesson->getDuration() * 5);
    }

    public function chargeType(): string
    {
        return "hourly rate";
    }
}

// listing 08.11
class FixedCostStrategy extends CostStrategy
{
    public function cost(Lesson $lesson): int
    {
        return 30;
    }
    public function chargeType(): string
    {
        return "fixed rate";
    }
}
    I can change the way that any Lesson object calculates cost by passing it a different
CostStrategy object at runtime. This approach then makes for highly flexible code.
Rather than building functionality into my code structures statically, I can combine and
recombine objects dynamically:

// listing 08.12
$lessons[] = new Seminar(4, new TimedCostStrategy());
$lessons[] = new Lecture(4, new FixedCostStrategy());

foreach ($lessons as $lesson) {
    print "lesson charge {$lesson->cost()}. ";
    print "Charge type: {$lesson->chargeType()}\n";
}
